title: Datamosh
description: Nine seconds of a rail journey in two shots, played through a video codec that runs live: an encoder and a decoder rebuilding every frame from the one before, block by block along real motion vectors, with residuals through an 8x8 DCT and an I-frame every three seconds and on the cut. Six seconds out of a summer train window, a slow lateral pan, then a hard cut to three seconds of winter track rushing at the camera out of a vanishing point. The decoder tunes in mid-stream, so the picture first assembles out of the paper from nothing but what moves. Press and hold and the I-frames and residuals stop reaching it. Hold over the cut and the winter shot's vectors arrive with nothing of their own to move: they push the summer picture instead, and the sky blooms out of the vanishing point over the whole frame, cloud pours down the sides in strips on the macroblock grid, and the rails are drawn in moving sky. Drag while you hold and the clip runs faster under your hand. Let go and a column of intra blocks sweeps it clean.
intent: Datamoshing as the actual codec process rather than a glitch shader, after Takeshi Murata's Monster Movie (2005, https://www.eai.org/titles/monster-movie) and Rosa Menkman's A Vernacular of File Formats (2010, https://li-ma.nl/article/vernacular-of-file-formats-summary), and herb's generative references 2 (a street photo whose region is smeared into strips while the rest stays intact) and 3 (real analog artefacts from a real signal model). Motion vectors are baked offline by block matching on the shipped VP9 frames (tools/depth/bakes/datamosh/mv.py: 16x16 macroblocks, 8x8 partitions where the SAD saving beats a split cost, hierarchical full search to +-56 px, H.264-style rate term toward the neighbours' median vector, half-pel refinement, intra where the best prediction is worse than DC), packed as per-MB modes plus median-predicted vector differences. Live in WebGL2 an encoder and a decoder run frame by frame: H.264 six-tap half-pel motion compensation, residual against the encoder's own reconstruction through a separable 8x8 DCT with a dead-zone quantiser (QP 30), closed loop, I-frames every 90 frames and wherever the stream carries a keyframe. The clip is two shots with a hard cut at frame 180, on an I-frame, so the I-frame a hold drops is a real scene change: the second shot (a forward run down a single track, every vector radial out of the vanishing point) moves the first shot's pixels, the reference/motion mismatch that makes a P-frame bloom. The seam back to the start is the same cut the other way: the lateral pan drags the winter picture sideways. The decoder joins between I-frames from blank paper; a hold drops its I-frames and lets the residual go within 0.2 s; a release runs an intra refresh across the macroblock columns. Stills: ?t=8&hold=4 holds across the cut; ?t=seconds stops the stream there, ?hold=seconds of hold before it, ?release=seconds before it lets go (the refresh mid-sweep), ?join=1 shows the opening, ?qp= sets the quantiser.

sources.author: ChristianBodhi
sources.note: 3840x2160, 30 fps, 27.2 s, out of a train window; location not given. Seconds 17.5-23.5 used (shot A), scaled to 1280x720 (Lanczos). Joined by a hard cut to shot B (below), then two-pass VP9 at 1.5 Mb/s with no alt-ref (clip.webm, 270 frames; libvpx keyframes at 0 and on the cut); motion vectors and modes baked from those decoded frames by tools/depth/bakes/datamosh/mv.py with a +-56 px search both ways (clip.mv, gzip).

sources.author: Bonaparcik
sources.note: 2048x922 as downloaded (2400x1080 original), 30 fps, 18 s, single track through pine forest in early winter, filmed out of the back of a train. Seconds 3-6 used (shot B, frames 180-269): cropped to 16:9 past the window pillar, scaled to 1280x720 and run backwards, so the line comes at the camera.
